paragraphs.heading: A slow swing of the axis
paragraphs.text: Axial precession is a slow, steady change in the direction that a spinning body's axis points, and gravity is what drives it. For Earth, it means the tilted axis gradually swings around, much as a spinning top wobbles. One full swing takes roughly 26,000 years. Over that time the axis sweeps out a double cone whose half-opening is about 23.4°. Astronomers call that angle the obliquity of the ecliptic.

paragraphs.heading: What pulls on Earth
paragraphs.text: Most of the motion comes from the Moon and the Sun. Their gravity tugs on the bulge around Earth's equator, and that tug moves the axis relative to space. This part is called lunisolar precession. A much smaller part, planetary precession, comes from nearby planets pulling Earth and its orbital plane slightly north or south, so the plane itself shifts a little. The lunisolar part is about 500 times larger, and the two together are called general precession.

paragraphs.heading: A changing north star
paragraphs.text: One effect you could see in the sky is that the north and south celestial poles crawl around in wide circles against the stars, finishing a lap in about 26,000 years. Today Polaris sits close to the north celestial pole, but it will not keep that job. In about 3,200 years Gamma Cephei, in the constellation Cepheus, takes over. The south celestial pole has no bright star at present, but over time precession will bring bright stars to that spot too.

paragraphs.heading: Seasons drift through the orbit
paragraphs.text: A second effect touches the calendar. The points in Earth's orbit where the solstices and equinoxes fall creep along at a nearly constant pace. Count one orbit from a June solstice, and the solstice comes around again about 20 minutes before Earth is back at the same place against the stars. So the tropical year, the cycle of the seasons, runs about 20 minutes short of the sidereal year, which is timed by the Sun's position among the stars. After about 26,000 years that gap grows to a whole year, and the seasons are back where they began in the orbit.

paragraphs.heading: How slow it is
paragraphs.text: The drift is tiny: about 50 arcseconds a year, which works out to 1 degree every 72 years. At today's pace one full circuit would take 25,772 years, which makes the tropical year shorter than the sidereal year by 1,224.5 seconds. The pace itself shifts a little over time. So no one can promise that the axis will sit exactly where it is now after 25,772 years.

paragraphs.heading: An old discovery
paragraphs.text: The effect was long called the precession of the equinoxes, because the equinoxes slid westward along the ecliptic against the fixed stars, the opposite way to the Sun's yearly motion. In the West its discovery is usually credited to Hipparchus, a Greek astronomer of the 2nd century BC from Rhodes or Nicaea. Ptolemy's Almagest records that Hipparchus measured where Spica and other bright stars sat in longitude. The word comes from the Latin praecedere, meaning to come before.
